claimBoundary: This is one provenance-bound Codex pass. It is single-model evidence, not human, instructor, independent, classroom, or multi-judge validation.

claims: A while loop repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.
After each pass through the body, the loop expression is evaluated again to decide whether to continue.
If the loop expression is true, the body runs again; if it is false, the loop terminates.
A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever — an infinite loop — so the body must make progress toward ending the condition.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §5.1 While loop

artifact.df: A loop that keeps running because its condition never turns false.
artifact.eg: A file-reading loop that never advances the file position can keep printing the same line forever.
artifact.mi: It is any loop that runs a lot of times.
artifact.cx: A loop can run many times and still end normally; it becomes infinite only when the stopping condition never changes.

artifact.df: A programming construct that repeats a block of code based on a specified criterion.
artifact.eg: Using a while loop to process user input until a specific command is entered.
artifact.mi: Thinking a loop only runs once per condition check.
artifact.cx: The construct repeatedly runs its body as long as a loop condition stays true, re-checking the condition before each iteration.

claims: A list is an ordered collection of values written in square brackets; each element has an index, beginning at 0.
A list is written with square brackets [] holding comma-separated values.
Individual elements are accessed directly using an index.
Indexes begin at 0 and end at one less than the length of the sequence.
A for loop can iterate through a list, visiting each element in order.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §3.4 List basics; §9.1 Modifying and iterating lists

artifact.df: The specific syntax used to define a list in Python.
artifact.eg: Defining a list as [10, 20, 30].
artifact.mi: Using parentheses () to define a collection of items.
artifact.cx: Using square brackets [] to define a list.

artifact.df: An ordered collection written with square brackets, where each element has an index.
artifact.eg: [3, 5, 8] is a list of three values, and 5 is at index 1.
artifact.mi: A common mistake is thinking the first position is index 1.
artifact.cx: Indexes begin at 0, so the first element is at index 0.

claims: Every Python value has a data type (such as int, float, or str); expressions combine values, and conversion functions move a value from one type to another.
The interpreter performs implicit type conversion to promote types automatically inside a mixed expression.
int() converts a value to an integer and removes any fractional part, so int(3.9) is 3.
True division (/) converts numbers to floats before dividing and always returns a float.
Floor division (//) computes the whole-number quotient, discarding the remainder.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §2.2 Type conversion; §2.5 Dividing integers

artifact.df: A change that turns a value from one data type into another.
artifact.eg: A trace of `int(3.9)` shows a float becoming an integer before the program keeps going.
artifact.mi: It only happens when the programmer writes an explicit conversion function.
artifact.cx: Python can also promote types automatically inside a mixed expression, and `int()` is one explicit way to convert.

artifact.df: The process of changing a value from one data type to another.
artifact.eg: Using int(3.9) results in 3.
artifact.mi: Believing that all operations automatically maintain the original data type.
artifact.cx: Explicitly using conversion functions like int() to change types.

claims: A class defines a type of object with attributes (data) and methods (behavior); it is a blueprint, and each object built from it is an instance.
A class is a blueprint for creating objects.
Individual objects created from a class are called instances.
Each instance carries its own copy of the attributes, while the methods defined by the class are shared by every instance.
attribution: OpenStax Introduction to Python Programming, §11.1 Object-oriented programming basics; §11.2 Classes and instances

artifact.df: A reusable blueprint that specifies what data and behavior objects will have.
artifact.eg: A course program might use a class to describe a bank account with balances and deposit actions.
artifact.mi: It is a single object already holding one set of values.
artifact.cx: A class is the source pattern; objects made from it are the instances.

artifact.df: A specific entity created from a class definition.
artifact.eg: A specific Car object created from the Car class is an instance.
artifact.mi: Confusing the class definition with the actual object created from it.
artifact.cx: Individual objects created from a class are called instances.

claims: Plate tectonics holds that Earth's rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that move over the ductile asthenosphere; most geologic action occurs at their three kinds of boundaries.
At divergent boundaries, lithospheric plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created.
At convergent boundaries, two or more plates move toward each other and lithosphere is destroyed.
At a transform boundary, plates slide horizontally past each other.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.4 Plate boundaries

artifact.q: A field map shows two oceanic plates separating and a broad band of fresh rock forming between them. Which boundary best matches this pattern?
artifact.ex: Divergent boundaries fit because plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created. A common misconception is to call any plate edge convergent, but convergence involves plates moving toward each other and destroying lithosphere instead.

artifact.q: Which boundary type is characterized by plates sliding horizontally past one another?
artifact.ex: The correct choice, Transform boundary, describes plates sliding horizontally past each other. A common misconception is confusing this with a divergent boundary, which involves plates moving away from each other.

claims: Igneous rock forms when molten magma or lava cools and crystallizes; how fast it cools controls crystal size, distinguishing coarse intrusive rocks from fine-grained extrusive rocks.
Lava cooling quickly at the surface forms tiny crystals, while magma cooling slowly at depth forms large crystals.
Magma that cools slowly deep within the crust forms intrusive (plutonic) rock with a coarse-grained texture.
Lava cooling at or near the surface forms extrusive (volcanic) rock with a fine-grained texture.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4.1 Magma generation and igneous textures

artifact.q: A magma body remains deep within the crust and cools slowly. What igneous texture should a student expect?
artifact.ex: Correct: coarse-grained plutonic texture, because slow cooling deep in the crust allows large crystals to grow. A plausible misconception is to link all cooling with tiny crystals, but that applies to rapid surface cooling of lava.

artifact.q: A rock with a fine-grained texture is typically formed by which cooling scenario?
op: Slow cooling deep within the crust.
Rapid cooling at or near the surface.
Rapid cooling deep within the crust.
artifact.ex: Rapid cooling at or near the surface. (Correct) This contrasts with the misconception that slow cooling at the surface produces fine-grained rock, as rapid cooling at the surface is the mechanism.

claims: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and an ordered crystal structure; minerals are identified by physical properties such as hardness, streak, luster, and cleavage.
Hardness is measured on the Mohs scale; diamond is a 10 and is about four times harder than corundum, a 9.
Streak is the color of a mineral's powder, and is more reliable than the color of the whole specimen.
Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes of weak bonding; minerals without such planes fracture irregularly.
Luster describes how a mineral's surface reflects light — metallic, glassy, or dull.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §3.1 What is a mineral; §3.5 Identifying minerals

artifact.q: If a mineral exhibits a tendency to break along flat planes of weak bonding, which property is being described?
artifact.ex: Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes of weak bonding. Misconception: Luster describes how a mineral's surface reflects light. Correct: Cleavage describes the tendency to break along flat planes of weak bonding.

artifact.q: A mineral sample breaks into thin, flat sheets along repeated smooth surfaces. Which description best matches that behavior?
artifact.ex: Cleavage is the tendency to break along flat planes of weak bonding. The most plausible misconception is to call any breakage a fracture, but fracture is irregular breakage when no such planes are present.

claims: The rock cycle describes how Earth's three rock families — igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic — form and continually transform into one another through geologic processes.
The rock cycle describes the major Earth materials, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other.
Igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid; lithified sediment becomes sedimentary rock; pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock.
If conditions melt the rocks into magma, the cycle begins anew with new igneous rocks.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4 The rock cycle

artifact.q: A student heats a buried sedimentary rock until minerals recrystallize without melting. Which rock family best fits the product?
artifact.ex: The best choice is metamorphic rock because pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock. A common misconception is to call any altered rock igneous, but igneous rock requires liquid rock to freeze solid; here, the rock changed without melting.

artifact.q: Which process is central to the rock cycle as described in the source material?
op: D) Ordering events in geologic time
artifact.ex: Option C is correct because the rock cycle describes how the three rock families form and transform into one another. Option A is a separate process related to surface change, and Option B is only one step in the cycle.

claims: The rock cycle describes how Earth's three rock families — igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic — form and continually transform into one another through geologic processes.
The rock cycle describes the major Earth materials, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other.
Igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid; lithified sediment becomes sedimentary rock; pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock.
If conditions melt the rocks into magma, the cycle begins anew with new igneous rocks.
attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4 The rock cycle

artifact.df: A description of Earth's main rock families and the processes that create and transform them.
artifact.eg: Magma cools into igneous rock, which can later become sedimentary or metamorphic rock.
artifact.mi: It is just a sequence of rock names.
artifact.cx: The cycle links igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks through geologic processes and can begin again if rocks melt into magma.

artifact.df: The continuous transformation of Earth's three rock families.
artifact.eg: A limestone layer being subjected to intense heat and pressure to become marble.
artifact.mi: Believing the rock cycle only involves the formation of igneous rocks.
artifact.cx: The cycle involves igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks continually transforming into one another.

claims: In music theory, a scale is "any consecutive series of notes that form a progression between one note and its octave", typically by order of pitch or fundamental frequency.
A measure of the width of each scale step provides a method to classify scales.
Scales can be abstracted from performance or composition.
Therefore, any scale is distinguishable by its "step-pattern", or how its intervals interact with each other.
A specific scale is defined by its characteristic interval pattern and by a special note, known as its first degree (or tonic).
The expression scale degree refers to these numerical labels.

artifact.tr: The defining feature that allows for the classification of a
artifact.df: A measure of the width of each scale step provides a method to classify scales.
artifact.eg: A scale with very wide steps is classified differently than one with narrow steps.
artifact.mi: Misconception: The width of the steps is the only factor determining the scale type.
artifact.cx: Correction: The measure of the width of each scale step provides a method to classify scales.

artifact.df: The first degree that anchors a specific scale.
artifact.eg: In C major, C is the tonic.
artifact.mi: It means the highest note in the octave.
artifact.cx: The tonic is the first degree, not the top pitch.

claims: In music, form refers to the structure of a musical composition or performance.
The term "binary form" is used to describe a musical piece with two sections that are about equal in length.
Musical form unfolds over time through the expansion and development of these ideas.
Form in music is the result of the interaction of the four structural elements described above [sound, harmony, melody, rhythm].
Subdivisions of each large musical unit are shown by lowercase letters (a, b, and so on).
The next level concerns the entire structure of any single self-contained musical piece or movement.

artifact.df: The overall structure of a musical composition or performance.
artifact.eg: A listener describes how a movement is organized from beginning to end.
artifact.mi: It means only the melody line.
artifact.cx: Form includes the full structure, not just one element like melody.

artifact.df: The overall arrangement of musical ideas within a piece.
artifact.eg: A sonata form movement.
artifact.mi: Thinking structure is the same as musical form.
artifact.cx: Musical form is the structure of a musical composition or performance.

claims: In music, form refers to the structure of a musical composition or performance.
The term "binary form" is used to describe a musical piece with two sections that are about equal in length.
Musical form unfolds over time through the expansion and development of these ideas.
Form in music is the result of the interaction of the four structural elements described above [sound, harmony, melody, rhythm].
Subdivisions of each large musical unit are shown by lowercase letters (a, b, and so on).
The next level concerns the entire structure of any single self-contained musical piece or movement.

artifact.df: A two-part design with sections of about equal length.
artifact.eg: A short piece divided into two roughly equal sections fits this description.
artifact.mi: It means any piece with two themes.
artifact.cx: The key feature is two sections that are about equal in length.

artifact.df: The result of the interaction of sound, harmony, melody, and rhythm.
artifact.eg: Examining how sound, harmony, melody, and rhythm interact to create the piece.
artifact.mi: A single musical element like rhythm.
artifact.cx: The interaction of the four structural elements described above [sound, harmony, melody, rhythm].

claims: In music, harmony is the concept of combining different sounds in order to create new, distinct musical ideas.
In these genres, chord progressions are the defining feature on which melody and rhythm are built.
Chord progressions are the foundation of harmony in Western musical tradition from the common practice era of classical music to the 21st century.
A first chord forms a 'progression' with a second chord, and a second with a third.
For example, the relative minor of C major is A minor, and in the key of A minor, the i, iv and v chords are A minor, D minor and E minor.
In many styles of popular and traditional music, chord progressions are expressed using the name and "quality" of the chords.

artifact.df: The structural base of harmony in Western music.
artifact.eg: The i, iv, and v chords in the key of A minor.
artifact.mi: Misconception: Thinking that only the melody establishes the harmonic foundation. Correction: The chord progression forms the foundation of harmony in Western musical tradition (Claim 2).
artifact.cx: The i, iv, and v chords in the key of A minor.

artifact.df: Combining different sounds so they form a new musical idea.
artifact.eg: A chord change that supports a melody in a song can show harmony at work.
artifact.mi: Harmony means only loudness or volume.
artifact.cx: It is not just one sound; it depends on sounds being combined in a musically meaningful way.

claims: Accessibility and usability evaluation combines standards-based conformance checks with observation of representative users completing realistic tasks.
WCAG organizes web accessibility around the principles perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust.
Evaluation with disabled and older users can find barriers that conformance evaluation alone does not reveal.
A usability test observes users attempting to use a product or service while thinking aloud.
A single disabled participant's experience should not be generalized to all people with disabilities.
sourceContext.license: W3C Document License and U.S. Government Work

artifact.df: A method of observing users attempting to use a product or service while thinking aloud.
artifact.eg: Watching a user struggle to find the 'submit' button on a prototype while verbalizing their confusion.
artifact.mi: Usability testing is just watching users without any verbal feedback.
artifact.cx: Usability testing is observing users attempting to use a product or service while thinking aloud (Claim 3).

artifact.df: A web-accessibility framework organized around four principles.
artifact.eg: A course team checks whether a prototype is perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust before user testing.
artifact.mi: It is mainly a checklist for visual design polish.
artifact.cx: The principles guide accessibility review beyond appearance and support structured conformance checks.

claims: Interactive prototyping builds a testable representation of how a planned experience looks and works without requiring every production detail.
Prototypes can be combined with usability testing or a cognitive walkthrough to test whether a design concept works.
Functional prototypes allow a team to observe how users interact with a product.
A prototype should show the major interactions even when not every interaction is functional.
Prototypes should support fast iteration and be inexpensive enough to discard after learning from them.

artifact.df: Building a testable representation of an intended experience that shows how it looks and works before every production detail exists.
artifact.eg: A team creates a clickable app mockup to check the main screen changes and button behavior before full development.
artifact.mi: It is the same as a finished product.
artifact.cx: A prototype is for learning and testing, and it may leave some details unfinished.

artifact.df: A preliminary model of an experience that can be used to verify design concepts.
artifact.eg: A low-fidelity wireframe used to test the flow of a new navigation menu.
artifact.mi: A testable representation must include every production detail.
artifact.cx: A testable representation builds a testable representation of how a planned experience looks and works without requiring every production detail.

claims: Journey mapping represents an end-to-end experience from the user's perspective so a team can see connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
A journey map should start from research about the steps users actually take and the transactions involved.
An experience map should make struggle points and candidate improvement areas visible.
A map can reveal dead ends where the user cannot continue toward the larger goal.
Journey analysis should include gaps between online and offline parts of a service.

artifact.df: A visual representation of the complete user path.
artifact.eg: Mapping the entire process from initial search to final purchase.
artifact.mi: Thinking a map only shows the main features.
artifact.cx: It shows connected steps, boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.

artifact.df: A research-backed way to chart the user's full experience from start to finish, including boundaries, breakdowns, and opportunities.
artifact.eg: In the capstone, students could map how someone signs up, submits a request, switches between web and phone support, and reaches the final outcome.
artifact.mi: It is just a flowchart of interface screens.
artifact.cx: The correction is that it focuses on the user's end-to-end experience, not only screens or system steps.
